title: Nonclustered Columnstore for Analytics
description: A rowstore GROUP BY scans in row mode; a nonclustered columnstore index enables batch-mode aggregation while the table still serves OLTP. Why it matters: being able to run fast analytics on the SAME table that serves live transactions (HTAP) is a genuinely valuable, modern architecture pattern worth knowing exists.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Most production databases exist to run one specific kind of workload well: fast, tiny, surgical operations — insert this order, look up that customer, update this row's status — the kind of work that happens thousands of times a minute in a live application. This style of workload has a name, **OLTP** (Online Transaction Processing), and the normal 'rowstore' table layout (every column of a row stored together, page by page) is genuinely the right tool for it, because a lookup by primary key only ever needs to grab one small row at a time.

The trouble starts when the *same* table also has to answer completely different kinds of questions: not 'give me order #48213' but 'across all half a million orders, how many are in each Status, and what's the total revenue per status?' That's an **analytical** question — it needs to sweep across every row but only cares about a couple of columns (`Status` and `Total`), and it wants a summary, not individual rows. Running that kind of aggregate query against a rowstore table forces SQL Server to drag every column of every row of the entire table through memory — all 500,000 full rows — just to pluck out two columns' worth of data from each one and add it up. It works, but it's enormously wasteful: you're paying the I/O and CPU cost of the whole row purely to reach two fields buried inside it.

The traditional answer to 'I need fast analytics over data that also serves live transactions' has historically been to build a *separate* system for it: a data warehouse, copied and reshaped from the transactional database on a schedule (nightly ETL jobs, ETL meaning Extract-Transform-Load — copy data out, reshape it, load it somewhere else). That works, but it means your analytics are always somewhat stale (only as fresh as the last copy job), it's extra infrastructure to build and maintain, and it duplicates storage. This lesson is about a more elegant option that SQL Server actually supports directly on the *same* table: a **nonclustered columnstore index (NCCI)**.

A columnstore index flips the storage model on its head for the columns it covers: instead of storing whole rows together, it stores each column's values packed together separately, and then compresses them heavily — because a column full of just `Status` values (a handful of repeating strings like 'Pending', 'Shipped', 'Cancelled') compresses extremely well when grouped together, the same way a list of the same few words repeated a thousand times compresses far better than a shuffled mix of everything. On top of the compression, columnstore unlocks **batch-mode execution** — instead of SQL Server processing one row at a time through each step of the query plan, it processes rows in big batches of roughly 900 at once, using CPU instructions that work on many values simultaneously rather than one-by-one. The combination of 'only touch the columns you need' plus 'heavily compressed' plus 'processed in big efficient batches' is what makes aggregations over a columnstore dramatically faster than the same aggregation over rowstore — often by an order of magnitude or more.

Here's the genuinely clever part, and the reason this lesson matters: a *nonclustered* columnstore index sits *alongside* the table's normal clustered rowstore index — it doesn't replace it. The original clustered index (organized by `OrderId`, say) keeps serving all the normal OLTP point lookups and updates exactly as before, completely unaffected. Meanwhile, SQL Server's optimizer is smart enough to recognize when a query is a good match for the columnstore copy of the data (like this GROUP BY) and automatically route it there instead of the rowstore, without you having to change the query at all — you just add the index, and the optimizer picks the best path for each query on its own. This gives you both worlds on one table: fast transactional operations *and* fast, always-fresh analytics, with no separate warehouse, no ETL lag, no duplicated infrastructure. This architecture pattern — serving both transactional and analytical workloads from the same live data — has a name in the industry: **HTAP** (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing), and it's considered a genuinely valuable, modern capability precisely because it collapses what used to require two separate systems into one.

What should tip you off that a table needs this? Watch for a **Clustered Index Scan** (reading every full row) feeding into a **Hash Match** or **Stream Aggregate** for a `GROUP BY`/aggregate query, especially when the query only actually touches a small number of the table's columns. The fix is to add a nonclustered columnstore index keyed on exactly the columns the analytic queries use — here, `Status` and `Total` — and let the optimizer automatically prefer scanning that columnstore copy (which shows up in the plan as an Index Scan on the columnstore index, running in batch mode) instead of the rowstore, while nothing about how the table serves ordinary transactional traffic changes at all.

## Scenario
The `Orders` table is a classic OLTP rowstore (clustered on `OrderId`). A reporting screen runs an analytical roll-up over all 500,000 rows:

```sql
SELECT Status, COUNT(*), SUM(Total) FROM Orders GROUP BY Status;
```

It does a full **Clustered Index Scan** plus a Hash Aggregate every time.

## Why it's slow
Rowstore stores whole rows together, so an aggregate over two columns still drags **every page of every row** through memory. That's fine for OLTP point lookups but wasteful for column-wide analytics.

## The fix: a nonclustered columnstore index (NCCI)
```sql
CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Orders ON Orders(Status, Total);
```

An NCCI stores just those columns **column-by-column**, heavily compressed, and unlocks **batch-mode** execution. The optimizer now answers the GROUP BY from the columnstore — no rowstore scan — while the clustered rowstore keeps serving transactional queries. This hybrid (HTAP) pattern gives you analytics speed without a separate copy of the data.

## What to look for
- Bad: a **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders`.
- Good: the plan reads **`NCCI_Orders`** instead (columnstore, batch mode).

> Note: columnstore scans surface in the plan as an *Index Scan* on the NCCI, and their I/O isn't counted as ordinary logical reads — so this lesson grades on the index used, not on `STATISTICS IO`.
startingQuery: SELECT Status, COUNT(*) AS Cnt, SUM(Total) AS Rev FROM Orders GROUP BY Status;
hints: The GROUP BY does a full Clustered Index Scan of the rowstore. Rowstore drags whole rows through memory even for a two-column aggregate.
A columnstore index stores columns separately, compressed, and enables batch-mode aggregation.
Add a nonclustered columnstore index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Orders ON Orders(Status, Total);
